keyVerseText: This Ezra went up from Babylon; and he was a ready scribe in the law of Moses, which the LORD God of Israel had given: and the king granted him all his request, according to the hand of the LORD his God upon him.
rootMeaning: The root of בַּקָּשָׁה (baqqâshâh) is בָּקַשׁ (bâqash), which carries the fundamental sense of seeking or requesting with intention and effort. This root implies more than a casual ask; it involves an active pursuit or striving to obtain something, often through inquiry or petition. The literal sense enriches the English term 'request' by highlighting the earnestness and deliberate seeking behind the act, especially in contexts of worship, prayer, or legal petitions.
usageInScripture: The word בַּקָּשָׁה appears eight times in Scripture, consistently translated as some form of request, petition, or entreaty. Common renderings such as 'thee and what is thy request' and 'all his request' indicate its use in formal or serious appeals, often directed to authority figures or God. This consistency shows that בַּקָּשָׁה denotes a respectful and purposeful asking, rather than a casual or trivial demand.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding בַּקָּשָׁה deepens our appreciation of prayer and petition in the life of faith, emphasizing that requests to God are not mere words but heartfelt seeking aligned with His will. It underscores the believer's active role in pursuing God's provision and guidance, reflecting dependence and trust. This term also reminds us that God honors sincere requests made in reverence and according to His purposes, as seen in the biblical narrative. The word thus enriches our view of the relational dynamic between God and His people, where seeking Him is both an act of faith and obedience.
keyVerseReflection: In Ezra 7:6, the phrase 'the king granted him all his request' highlights the power and efficacy of a well-founded petition. Here, בַּקָּשָׁה conveys not just a simple ask but a formal and earnest entreaty that aligns with God's hand upon Ezra. This word reveals that Ezra's requests were not arbitrary but divinely supported, showing how God can work through earthly authorities to fulfill the desires of His faithful servants.
